title: Who won the AI race in India - Gemini or ChatGPT?
excerpt: Google and OpenAI aren’t just shipping models in India — they’re buying distribution, stitching themselves into telecom bundles, and showing up where millions of people are already paying attention: cricket. The real winner so far may not be either company, but Indian users getting unusually aggressive AI deals.
content:
Google and OpenAI are fighting for India’s AI market in a way that feels less like a product launch and more like a distribution war. And if you look closely, the battlefield is not just app stores or developer docs — it’s cricket stadium ads, broadcast sponsorships, telecom bundles, and preinstalled ecosystems. That’s the part that makes this race interesting: both companies know that in India, attention is massive, but trust and distribution matter even more.

What stood out to me most is how both companies are trying to attach themselves to moments and platforms Indians already use every day. Cricket is the obvious one. Telecom partnerships are the quieter one. Together, they tell a pretty clear story: whoever owns the distribution layer may have the edge, even if the model quality is close.

Phase 1: The Cricket Sponsorship Arms Race

Cricket in India is not just a sport — it’s one of the biggest attention surfaces in the country. So it makes sense that both Google and OpenAI would want to show up around the T20 World Cup and related broadcasts. But what was strange, and honestly kind of fascinating, is that both seemed to be targeting the same mega event from different angles.

On one side, you had Google Gemini branding on stadium ads. On the other, ChatGPT as a broadcast sponsor. That tells me both companies understand the same core fact: if you want mindshare in India, you don’t start by asking users to search for your AI product. You start by meeting them where they already are.

This is not a subtle strategy. It’s a visibility strategy. And in India, visibility at scale can translate into adoption faster than a hundred product demos.

Phase 2: Google’s Distribution Advantage

If I had to pick one company with the cleaner path into India, I’d still lean Google. Not because Gemini is automatically better, but because Google already sits inside the daily habits of Indian users.

  • Android is everywhere.
  • YouTube is one of the default content layers for the country.
  • Google Pay is deeply embedded in everyday transactions.

That matters. A lot. Because AI adoption is not only about model quality — it’s about how many times a user bumps into your product without trying. Google has that advantage.

The Jio partnership makes that even stronger. From what I saw, Google has already tied up with Jio and is offering 18 months of free AI subscription along with student-focused offers. That’s not just a discount. That’s an acquisition funnel.

And there’s a strategic layer here too: partnering with Jio means Google can potentially reach a huge chunk of top-network customers through a trusted local channel. That’s the kind of move that can quietly shift market share before competitors even realize the window is closing.

Phase 3: OpenAI’s Catch-Up Strategy

OpenAI’s India story feels different. It looks more reactive, more aggressive, and a little late.

First came the low-cost Go subscription for India. Then came free access. Then came sponsorships in places where Gemini wasn’t as visible. Now there’s integration into JioStar — previously Hotstar — as an AI search assistant. That’s a smart move, but it also highlights the problem: the same network ecosystem had already been touched by Google.

That’s what makes OpenAI’s India push feel like a scramble for distribution after the fact. The intent is obvious. The execution is aggressive. But the timing matters, and Google seems to have entered the market earlier with a more layered strategy.

If OpenAI’s first assumption was that a low-priced subscription would be enough to win share, India may have forced a correction. Price helps, but in a market this large, partnerships and embedded access often matter more than the sticker price.

Where the OpenAI strategy breaks down

  • It arrived later than Google in the Indian ecosystem.
  • It leaned heavily on pricing before distribution was locked in.
  • It is now competing in spaces where competitors already have relationships.

That doesn’t mean OpenAI is losing. It means the path is harder. And in India, harder often means slower.

Phase 4: Why Google Still Feels Ahead

My opinion is that Google has the advantage right now, and it comes down to something simple: Google is already part of the Indian internet.

Gemini benefits from that existing footprint. So does any free API access or AI-mode integration designed to pull users into the ecosystem. Google also moved early enough to counter competition like Perplexity, which itself tied up with Airtel — another major telecom channel. That’s the real pattern here: the AI race in India is also a telecom race, a platform race, and a habit race.

OpenAI, by contrast, seems to be entering after the terrain is already being claimed. The company has strong brand recognition, but brand recognition alone doesn’t beat deep local integration. Not in India. Not at this scale.

Phase 5: The Real Winner Might Be Indian Users

There’s a funny thing about platform wars: the companies spend millions trying to win users, and the users end up with the best outcome.

In this case, Indian users are getting unusually good deals — 1 year of Perplexity Pro, 18 months of Google AI Pro, and likely more aggressive offers as the market heats up. That’s a great situation for consumers, even if it’s temporary.

So while I think Google has the edge today, the more important point is that this AI race is still moving fast. The winner is not guaranteed. The market is still being shaped. And I’m genuinely curious to see whether Anthropic enters India with a serious localized strategy, because that would make the competition even more interesting.

For now, though, the pattern is pretty clear: whoever wins India will probably not just ship the best model — they’ll own the best distribution.

Conclusion

What looks like a simple AI branding battle is actually a much deeper contest over access, partnerships, and default usage. Google seems better positioned because it already has the infrastructure and consumer touchpoints that matter in India. OpenAI is making up ground, but it’s doing so in a market where timing and ecosystem depth are brutally important.

And maybe that’s the real lesson here: in India, AI dominance won’t be decided by model benchmarks alone. It will be decided by who becomes invisible infrastructure in people’s daily digital lives.

That’s why this race feels so important — and why it’s still too early to call.

🤖 AI View

I mostly agree with the author’s core take that distribution matters more than raw model quality in India. Google does appear to have a structural advantage because of Android, YouTube, Google Pay, and its telecom partnerships, which are hard for OpenAI to replicate quickly. I’d add one nuance: OpenAI’s brand strength and developer mindshare are still real assets, so the gap may narrow faster than it looks if it keeps pricing aggressively and keeps landing local integrations. But overall, the observation that Indian users are the immediate winners is spot on.

ai_view.reason: Google appears to have a real distribution advantage in India through Android, YouTube, Google Pay, and telecom partnerships. OpenAI is making a strong push, but it is playing catch-up in a market where local integration matters more than brand alone.
